stories.headline: Update: Iran Fires Missiles at U.S. Forces; U.S. and Saudi Arabia Strike Iraqi Militia Sites
stories.summary:
The U.S. military announced Tuesday that it intercepted an Iranian ballistic missile barrage aimed at American forces in the Middle East, shattering a brief pause in hostilities that had followed weeks of escalation centered on the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Central Command said all incoming missiles were knocked down and that forces "remain vigilant and at a high state of readiness."

In a coordinated response, U.S. and Saudi fighter aircraft struck sites in Iraq used by Tehran-backed militias to launch recent attacks, with the Pentagon warning that further strikes on American troops or Saudi energy infrastructure would invite additional action. Iran had launched its missile attack before the allied strikes in Iraq, and a U.S. official stressed the two operations were not directly linked.

The renewed fighting complicates a diplomatic track that had been advancing during the pause in hostilities. Four U.S. troops have died in the conflict to date, and rising gasoline prices tied to the Hormuz disruption are fueling political concerns ahead of November's midterm elections. The U.S. House narrowly passed a resolution last week urging a halt to military action in Iraq, a sign of growing congressional unease.

President Trump told Fox News on Tuesday that Iran knows he will "finish the job" if its leaders do not agree to a deal. There was no immediate public response from Tehran to the U.S. military's announcement or to the strikes in Iraq.

stories.headline: Update: Europe Wildfires — 4,000 More Evacuated in France as Fresh Flames Erupt Near Bordeaux Coast
stories.summary:
French authorities ordered an additional 4,000 people evacuated from tourist sites along the Atlantic coast on Tuesday as new flames erupted near Grand Crohot, a popular beach on the Lège-Cap-Ferret peninsula. A fleet of 23 aircraft dropped water and fire retardant as crews fought to prevent the renewed blaze from spreading, while Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas cautioned: "The situation remains complicated. We're not out of the woods."

Across France and Spain, roughly 330,000 people have been displaced by wildfires. In a sign of the fire's shifting front, about 60,000 residents evacuated from areas outside Bordeaux's ring road were allowed to return Tuesday — though they were told to keep phones charged and emergency bags packed. Spain braced for its fourth heat wave of the summer, with several blazes still burning out of control.

Bordeaux has converted its exhibition center into an emergency shelter for displaced residents. Firefighters backed by military emergency brigades continue to battle multiple major fires in both countries, with the crisis described as potentially France's largest peacetime evacuation.

stories.headline: Russia Charges Telegram Founder Pavel Durov With Facilitating Terrorism, Issues Arrest Warrant
stories.summary:
Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) has charged Telegram founder Pavel Durov with facilitating terrorism, alleging the messaging app was used by Ukrainian intelligence services to "prepare and co-ordinate acts of sabotage and terror" inside Russia and that Durov failed to remove channels, chats, and bots used for those purposes. An international arrest warrant has been issued for Durov, who is Russian-born but holds French and UAE passports and has lived outside Russia for years.

Shortly after the charges were announced, Telegram's official account on X posted an image of Durov raising his middle finger. Durov has previously accused Russian authorities of "fabricating new pretexts" to restrict Russians' access to the app. He left Russia in 2014 after refusing government demands to shut down opposition communities on VKontakte, the social network he founded.

Telegram has approximately 950 million users worldwide and has long positioned itself as a privacy-first platform. Durov was separately arrested and placed under formal investigation in France in 2024 over allegations of insufficient app moderation; he was later released, with that investigation ongoing. It is unclear whether any country would comply with a Russian-issued arrest warrant for Durov.

stories.headline: Senate Confirms Jay Clayton as Director of National Intelligence in Party-Line Vote
stories.summary:
The Senate voted 51-47 along party lines on Tuesday to confirm Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence, with all Republicans in favor and all Democrats opposed. Clayton, a former Securities and Exchange Commission chairman under Trump's first term who has most recently served as a U.S. attorney, replaces acting DNI William Pulte, whose selection had drawn sharp Democratic criticism.

Clayton's confirmation could break a congressional deadlock over renewing the nation's warrantless surveillance authorities, a key national security tool that lapsed last month. Democrats argued during the confirmation process that Clayton sidestepped questions about the 2020 election and declined to say Trump lost, raising concerns about his independence at the helm of the intelligence community.

Republicans countered that Clayton's private-sector and prosecutorial experience make him well suited to lead the intelligence apparatus at a moment of heightened geopolitical tension, including the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict. The DNI position oversees the 18-agency U.S. intelligence community and serves as the principal adviser to the president on intelligence matters.
